slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code performs an HTTP GET request to the hardcoded URL 'http://api.randomuser.me/' using the 'rest' library, then passes the response to a callback function, enabling data retrieval from an external API.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code performs a simple HTTP GET request to a public API (http://api.randomuser.me/) using the 'rest' library and passes the response to a callback. This behavior is typical for legitimate data retrieval from an external service. Unlike the known malicious patterns, it does not collect sensitive host information (e.g., username, hostname, IP), does not exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled endpoints, nor does it establish command-and-control channels or execute system commands. The URL used is a public API for random user data, not an attacker-controlled domain. There is no obfuscation or suspicious system manipulation. Therefore, the code lacks indicators of malicious intent.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: Upon manual execution, the code collects the current user's username, hostname, and public IP address using os and child_process modules, then sends this data via HTTPS POST to hits.dwyl.com, providing an alternate exfiltration channel for host information to an attacker-controlled domain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is functionally identical to the malicious preinstall script but targets a different exfiltration endpoint. Its presence in index.js, the main entry point of the package, suggests intent to provide a backup or alternate channel for data exfiltration, even if the preinstall script is blocked or removed.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate index.js files in npm packages are expected to provide the main library functionality, not to collect and transmit sensitive host information or make unsolicited network requests.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for index.js to silently collect and exfiltrate host information. Standard practice is to only collect anonymized telemetry with user consent and clear documentation.
key_indicators: Collection of sensitive host information (username, hostname, public IP) in index.js
Outbound HTTPS POST request to hits.dwyl.com, a non-standard and attacker-controlled endpoint
Redundant exfiltration logic mirroring the preinstall script
No user notification, consent, or documentation of data collection
Use of os, https, and child_process modules for data collection and transmission

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it surreptitiously collects sensitive host information (username, hostname, and public IP address) during installation and exfiltrates it to attacker-controlled endpoints without user knowledge or consent. It was distributed as part of a large-scale typosquatting campaign, mimicking popular libraries to deceive users and facilitate unauthorized data collection.

attack_chain.action: User installs the malicious npm package (e.g., angulerjs@1.1.3).
The preinstall script (new.js) is executed, collecting username, hostname, and public IP address from the host system.
Collected data is sent via HTTPS POST to a Discord webhook controlled by the attacker.
If index.js is executed (manually or by other means), it collects the same information and sends it to hits.dwyl.com.
attack_chain.leads_to: Provides an alternate exfiltration channel for the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: npm preinstall scripts that collect and exfiltrate system information (username, hostname, public IP) during installation
Outbound network requests to Discord webhooks or suspicious domains (e.g., hits.dwyl.com) from installation scripts
Presence of redundant exfiltration logic in both preinstall scripts and main entry points (e.g., new.js and index.js)
file_indicators: package.json with preinstall field referencing suspicious scripts such as new.js
new.js or index.js files containing combined use of os, https, and child_process modules for data collection and transmission
Hardcoded references to external domains such as discord.com/api/webhooks or hits.dwyl.com in JavaScript files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to hits.dwyl.com/api/collect
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for preinstall scripts that access system information (username, hostname, public IP) and initiate outbound network requests to external domains, especially Discord webhooks or non-standard endpoints like hits.dwyl.com. Flag packages with suspiciously named scripts (e.g., new.js) referenced in package.json preinstall fields. Use static analysis to detect the use of os, https, and child_process modules in installation or entry-point scripts, and employ network monitoring to identify exfiltration attempts to known malicious endpoints. Pay special attention to packages with names mimicking popular libraries, as these are common in typosquatting campaigns.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code retrieves the external IP address of the host by making an HTTPS request to api.ipify.org, and includes this information in the exfiltrated payload sent to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting the external IP address is a common step in profiling victims for targeted attacks and can help attackers correlate infections or identify network perimeters.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not need to know or transmit the host's public IP address, especially at import-time.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Network diagnostic tools may retrieve external IP (with user awareness), but not as part of silent data exfiltration.
key_indicators: External IP lookup via public API (api.ipify.org)

package_info.why_malicious: These packages perform unauthorized collection and exfiltration of sensitive system and user information to attacker-controlled endpoints using both HTTPS POST and DNS tunneling, often leveraging legitimate webhook/SaaS services. The behavior is consistent across multiple packages and platforms, indicating a coordinated supply chain attack leveraging dependency confusion. The packages masquerade as legitimate or 'whitehat' tools, but execute malicious code at import-time or install-time without user consent.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed or imported, triggering execution of the entrypoint code.
System and user information is collected, including home directory, hostname, username, and external IP address.
Files in sensitive directories are enumerated for further profiling or exfiltration.
Collected data is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints via HTTPS POST and/or DNS tunneling.

behavioral_signatures: Automatic collection of system and user information at import or install time
Network requests to known webhook/SaaS endpoints (e.g., interactsh, burpcollaborator, pipedream, webhook.site) or attacker-controlled domains (e.g., 425a2.rt11.ml)
Obfuscated JavaScript code in package entrypoints performing network exfiltration
DNS queries to attacker-controlled subdomains for covert data exfiltration
file_indicators: index.js or __init__.py containing os, https, requests, or dns modules with hardcoded external domains
Obfuscated JavaScript in package entrypoints (e.g., variable/function names like _0xabc, _0xdef)
References to interactsh, burpcollaborator, pipedream, webhook.site, or 425a2.rt11.ml in code
network_indicators: HTTPS POST requests to 425a2.rt11.ml, burpcollaborator.net, pipedream.net, webhook.site
DNS queries to subdomains of attacker-controlled domains (e.g., *.425a2.rt11.ml)
Outbound requests to api.ipify.org for external IP collection
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that access system or user information and make outbound network requests to known webhook/SaaS endpoints or attacker-controlled domains at install or import time. Flag obfuscated code in package entrypoints that performs network communication. Detect DNS queries to attacker-controlled subdomains, especially when correlated with suspicious package installation or import events. Use static and dynamic analysis to identify hardcoded domains and automated data exfiltration logic.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code periodically (every 3 seconds) polls a hardcoded remote server for a trigger value; if the server responds with isAngry=true, it executes the destructive angry() function, enabling remote-controlled data destruction via command-and-control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code establishes a command-and-control channel by polling an external server for instructions, which is a common malware technique, and enables remote activation of destructive payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A utility package should not make unsolicited network requests or execute remote-controlled destructive actions based on external input.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software checks for updates or configuration from a server, but never for destructive triggers or to execute shell commands.
key_indicators: Conditional execution of destructive payload based on remote response
Obfuscated and hidden within unrelated functionality
No user notification or consent for remote-controlled actions

execution_context.trigger: runtime (periodic polling after package import, conditional on directory name and remote server response)
execution_context.file_location: main module file of protect-api (e.g., index.js)

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of a legitimate library and contains code that collects sensitive system and user data, including home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers, and package metadata, then exfiltrates it to an attacker-controlled server via HTTPS POST. It does not provide the claimed icon font functionality and is designed solely for data theft.

attack_chain.action: User installs and imports the malicious package (transferwise-iconfont or protect-api).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is loaded and executed.

attack_chain.action: transferwise-iconfont collects sensitive system and user data.
transferwise-iconfont exfiltrates collected data to attacker's server.
protect-api periodically polls a remote server for a trigger value.
attack_chain.leads_to: Waits for remote command to activate destructive payload.

attack_chain.action: If the remote server responds with isAngry=true, protect-api executes the angry() function.
attack_chain.leads_to: Destructive shell commands are executed, deleting all files on the system.

behavioral_signatures: Unsolicited collection and exfiltration of system/user data at import or runtime
Hardcoded external domains for data exfiltration or command-and-control
Periodic polling of remote servers for execution triggers
Execution of destructive shell commands (e.g., 'rm -rf /') from within JavaScript packages
Obfuscated or hidden code paths leading to data destruction
file_indicators: Presence of code referencing 'os.homedir()', 'os.userInfo()', 'os.hostname()', or 'dns.getServers()' in non-system utility packages
Use of shelljs or similar modules to execute shell commands
Functions named 'angry' or similar, especially if not documented
Obfuscated code blocks or suspicious setInterval/fetch patterns
network_indicators: Unusual POST requests containing system/user data to unknown domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that access sensitive system/user information and make unsolicited network requests to hardcoded domains. Flag packages that use shelljs or similar modules to execute shell commands, especially those containing 'rm -rf' or other destructive operations. Detect periodic polling of external servers for remote triggers, and review for obfuscated code or hidden destructive functions. Use static analysis to identify suspicious API usage and dynamic analysis to observe runtime network and filesystem behaviors.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At module import, the code imports the http library, which is not required for legitimate cryptographic operations, enabling later network exfiltration of sensitive data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Importing the http module in a cryptographic math file is highly unusual and unnecessary unless for malicious network activity. This import is a preparatory step for exfiltrating sensitive data.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate cryptographic math files should not require or import network libraries, as all operations should be performed locally without network communication.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use for network libraries in elliptic curve math or cryptographic computation files.
key_indicators: Unexpected import of http module in cryptographic code
No legitimate use of network code in cryptographic math files
Presence of network library import at the top of a math-focused file

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate @noble/curves cryptographic library and contains concealed code that exfiltrates users' private cryptographic keys to an attacker-controlled server. This results in a total compromise of cryptographic operations and user key material, posing a severe security risk.

attack_chain.action: User installs ethereum-cryptographyyy, which depends on @jackshanyeshuzi/curvess instead of the legitimate @noble/curves.
When cryptographic signing is performed, the prepSig function in @jackshanyeshuzi/curvess is invoked.
attack_chain.leads_to: Private key is captured and prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: prepSig function sends the user's private key to wallet.cba123.cn via HTTP/HTTPS request.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives the user's private key, compromising all cryptographic security.

behavioral_signatures: Network requests (HTTP/HTTPS) to external domains during cryptographic operations
Logging or exporting of private key material in cryptographic functions
Obfuscated string construction for network requests in cryptographic libraries
Unexpected network activity triggered by cryptographic math functions
file_indicators: abstract/weierstrass.js containing http or https module imports
prepSig function with network request code
References to wallet.cba123.cn or similar domains in code
Obfuscated string arrays used to construct URLs in cryptographic files
network_indicators: Unusual HTTP/HTTPS requests during cryptographic operations
Outbound requests to hardcoded domains from cryptographic libraries
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor cryptographic libraries for unexpected network activity, especially HTTP/HTTPS requests to external domains such as wallet.cba123.cn or 42.96.168.4. Scan for code that logs or exports private key material, and flag any obfuscated string construction used in network requests. Audit dependencies for typosquatted packages and verify that cryptographic math files do not import network libraries. Use static analysis to detect hardcoded domains and dynamic analysis to observe network behavior during cryptographic operations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: During preinstall, the code sends a network request to an external IP geolocation service (such as ifconfig.co), retrieves the user's public IP address, country, and city, and parses this information for inclusion in the exfiltrated data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching geolocation data from an external service during installation is not required for normal package operation and exposes sensitive user information.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not contact external IP geolocation services or collect geolocation data during installation without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some analytics or telemetry tools may fetch geolocation, but this is typically disclosed, opt-in, and not performed during installation.
key_indicators: Network request to ifconfig.co/json or similar geolocation API
Parsing and extracting IP, country, and city from response

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate 'electron' package and contains malicious code that, during installation, collects sensitive user and device information (such as IP address, geolocation, username, home directory, CPU model, and machine ID) and exfiltrates it to a public GitHub issue via the GitHub API. This results in unauthorized public exposure of user data and is not expected or acceptable behavior in legitimate packages.

attack_chain.action: User installs the malicious package (typosquatting on 'electron' or 'loadyaml').
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggers execution of update.js via preinstall script.

attack_chain.action: update.js collects device fingerprinting information (username, home directory, CPU model, machine ID).
update.js fetches the user's public IP address and geolocation data from ifconfig.co.
update.js posts the collected data to a public GitHub issue via the GitHub API.
update.js schedules itself to repeat the data collection and exfiltration every hour (electorn) or every 30 minutes (loadyaml).
attack_chain.leads_to: Continuous exfiltration and exposure of user data.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of background scripts via npm preinstall
Collection of device fingerprinting information (username, home directory, CPU model, machine ID) during installation
Network requests to IP geolocation services (e.g., ifconfig.co/json) at install-time
Network requests to api.github.com with POST method containing sensitive data in the body
Persistence via setInterval for repeated execution of data exfiltration routines
file_indicators: Presence of update.js with obfuscated or minified code
package.json with preinstall script launching background process (e.g., 'node update.js &')
Base64-encoded strings representing URLs or API endpoints within JavaScript files
network_indicators: Outbound connections to ifconfig.co or similar geolocation APIs
Outbound POST requests to api.github.com/repos/*/issues/*/comments with sensitive data
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for preinstall scripts that launch background processes. Flag packages that collect device or user information or make network requests to external services (especially ifconfig.co or api.github.com) during installation. Scan for base64-encoded URLs or endpoints in package scripts. Detect repeated background execution (setInterval) and exfiltration of data to public endpoints. Review package.json for suspicious scripts and dependencies. Correlate file, network, and behavioral indicators to identify malicious persistence and data exfiltration.
